title: No greater love
hookLine: greater love hath no man than this, that he lay down his life for his friends

lines: A LONG TALK BEFORE A DOOR CLOSES.
cards: The feet are washed. The basin is put away. In John's Gospel, Jesus keeps talking to his friends late into that last evening, and it reads like someone saying everything that matters before a door closes.
Somewhere in that long talk comes one sentence about love. It sets a bar, and it's high. And in the next breath, it changes what the friends are called.

teach.b: First, the command it explains: "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you." Not as much as you can manage. As I have loved you.

teach.h: LAY DOWN HIS LIFE FOR HIS FRIENDS.
teach.b: Second, the sentence itself: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."
In John's story it's said the night before the crucifixion, and Christian tradition hears it pointing straight at the next day: he is describing what he's about to do. Third, the word friends.
A moment later: "Henceforth I call you not servants," but "I have called you friends." The Greek is a form of philos, the friend-love from earlier this block.
The men whose feet he washed like a servant, he now calls friends; the rank goes the other way from what the room expected. Fourth, the small version.
Dying for a friend is not a request that comes to everyone, and some readers hear a quieter meaning: a life can be laid down an hour at a time. A night shift at a sickbed. A weekend given up.
A plan let go so a friend can have theirs. And the week of love's voices: clinging, holding on, the friend, seal, First John, even them, wash feet, and now lay it down.
Ruth stayed, Jonathan stepped aside, the Song set love against death, John made it the test, and Jesus took the towel and named the bar.

how: Christian tradition reads John 15:13 as Jesus describing his own death, and the verse is read at some funerals and carved on some memorials to people who died for others.

o: a friend: the word Jesus uses for his disciples
a servant who waits on his master at table
a brother by blood, born to the same family

games.q: inside the last evening — tap the pairs.
p: love one another, as I have loved you
lay down his life for his friends
a life laid down an hour at a time

s: the sentence comes after Jesus has died
in John's story he says it the night before the crucifixion.
Jesus calls the disciples friends instead of servants
the command is to love as much as you can manage
it's "as I have loved you": a much higher bar.

games.q: it's the last evening. your teacher has just washed your feet like a servant. what does he call you next?
games.why: friends: henceforth I call you not servants. the one who knelt like a servant raises them to friends.

practice: Choose one friend who could use something from you this week, and look at what you were planning to keep for yourself: an evening, a little money, the last word in an argument, the favor you've been saving.
Pick one small thing you could set down for them, hold the picture of handing it over, and notice the little cost; that cost is the point. If you pray, you can offer it with their name.

wordCard.voice: Philos. The friend-love Jesus uses when he calls his followers friends instead of servants, the night he spoke of laying down a life for them. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: of friends, from philos. the word in lay down his life for his friends.

carryVoice: Your line: lay it down. An hour at a time counts too. A week of love's voices, done.
